posts.title: Getting Started with React Hooks
posts.body:
React Hooks changed the way we write components forever. Before hooks, managing state and side-effects required class components with all their boilerplate. Now, useState and useEffect let us do the same things in just a few lines of clean functional code.

The most important hooks to learn first are useState for local state, useEffect for side-effects like data fetching, and useContext for consuming shared state. Once you are comfortable with those three, everything else clicks into place quickly.

posts.title: Why TypeScript Is Worth the Learning Curve
posts.body:
I resisted TypeScript for over a year. Adding types to JavaScript felt like unnecessary overhead. Then I joined a project with 80,000 lines of untyped code and spent three days tracking down a bug caused by a misspelled property name.

TypeScript catches entire categories of bugs at compile time that would otherwise only show up in production. Autocomplete becomes genuinely useful, refactoring is safe, and onboarding new teammates takes half the time. The learning curve is real but short. Give it two weeks and you will never go back.

posts.title: Building a REST API with Express and Node.js
posts.body:
Node.js and Express remain one of the fastest ways to spin up a working REST API. In under an hour you can have endpoints for creating, reading, updating, and deleting resources, with JSON responses and basic error handling.

The key things to get right early are clear route naming that reflects your resource hierarchy, centralised error handling middleware, and input validation before anything touches your database. Skip any one of these and debugging becomes painful fast.

posts.title: Understanding JavaScript Closures Once and for All
posts.body:
Closures are one of those JavaScript concepts that trips people up repeatedly even after years of experience. A closure is simply a function that remembers the variables from the scope where it was defined, even after that outer scope has finished executing.

The classic gotcha is using var in a loop. Because var is function-scoped, all the loop iterations share the same variable. Switching to let, or wrapping each iteration in its own function, fixes the problem immediately. Understanding closures also unlocks understanding of module patterns, memoization, and most React hooks internals.

posts.title: CSS Grid: Stop Fighting Your Layouts
posts.body:
Before CSS Grid, building a two-dimensional layout meant fighting floats, clearfixes, and a parade of hacks. Flexbox improved things enormously for one-dimensional layouts, but Grid is what makes page-level layout genuinely straightforward.

The two properties you will use most are grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows. Define your columns with fr units, name your grid areas, and your layout almost writes itself. The most important mental shift is thinking about the entire layout container first instead of positioning individual elements.

posts.title: The Git Commands Every Developer Actually Uses
posts.body:
You do not need to memorise every Git command. After years of daily use, my real workflow comes down to about fifteen commands. The ones that matter most are commit, branch, merge, rebase, stash, and log with some useful flags.

The two commands that save me the most time are git stash for quickly switching context without losing work, and git log --oneline --graph --all for getting a clear picture of the branch history. Learn those two well and your Git life gets dramatically simpler.

posts.title: 10 VS Code Extensions I Cannot Work Without
posts.body:
A well-configured VS Code can feel like a superpower. Over the years I have settled on a small set of extensions that I install immediately on any new machine.

The essentials: ESLint and Prettier for code quality, GitLens for blame and history at a glance, Path Intellisense for autocompleting import paths, and Error Lens for showing errors inline without having to hover. If you write TypeScript, the TypeScript Hero extension handles import organisation automatically, which alone saves several minutes every day.

posts.title: 10 Days in Japan: Everything They Did Not Tell Me
posts.body:
Japan was the first country that genuinely overwhelmed me with how different it was from anything I expected. The food, the transit system, the unspoken social rules, the sheer density of things to see in a single city block.

Tokyo alone could take a month. I spent three days there and barely scratched the surface. Kyoto was the emotional highlight, particularly the bamboo grove at Arashiyama at 6am before the crowds arrived. The one thing nobody warned me about: carry cash everywhere. Japan is still surprisingly cash-dependent outside of major tourist areas.

posts.title: How I Travelled Europe for Six Weeks on a Tight Budget
posts.body:
European travel has a reputation for being expensive, but with the right approach you can stretch your money much further than most guides suggest. The key is being flexible with dates, using overnight trains when possible to save on accommodation, and eating where locals eat rather than anywhere with a menu in six languages.

Hostel dorms in eastern Europe cost under 12 euros a night. Interrail passes make crossing borders almost effortless. The biggest hidden cost most people miss is tourist attractions. Many of Europe's best museums have free days or free hours. Research before you go and you can cut your sightseeing budget in half.

posts.title: What Solo Travel Taught Me About Myself
posts.body:
The idea of travelling alone scared me for years. No safety net, no one to consult, no one to share the weird moments with. I finally booked a solo trip almost on a whim and it became one of the most important things I have ever done.

When you travel alone you make every decision yourself. You eat when you are hungry, stop when something interests you, and change your plans without negotiating. You also talk to strangers far more than you would otherwise, because you have to. Some of the most meaningful conversations of my life happened because I was eating lunch alone and someone sat down next to me.

posts.title: Portugal's Alentejo Region: The Countryside They Keep Secret
posts.body:
Everyone goes to Lisbon and Porto. The Alentejo region in southern Portugal is where the Portuguese actually go on holiday. Rolling plains dotted with cork oak trees, medieval walled villages, and some of the best wine in the country at prices that feel almost absurd.

Evora is the obvious starting point, with its Roman temple and bone chapel, but the smaller villages like Monsaraz and Marvao are where you feel the real pace of life. The food is hearty and unfussy: grilled lamb, thick soups, fresh sheep's cheese. If you want to experience Portugal without the crowds, head south.

posts.title: The Perfect Homemade Pizza: It Is All About the Dough
posts.body:
I spent most of last year on an obsessive quest for a perfect homemade pizza. I tried dozens of dough recipes, experimented with different flours, and burned more than a few attempts. Eventually I narrowed it down to three things that actually matter: high-protein flour, a cold slow ferment of at least 48 hours, and a very hot oven.

Most home ovens top out at 250 degrees which is not really hot enough. Preheating your oven with a baking steel or thick cast iron tray for a full hour gets you much closer to what a proper pizza oven produces. The difference in crust texture is remarkable.

posts.title: The Food Markets of Morocco: A Sensory Education
posts.body:
Nothing prepares you for the medina in Fez or the Djemaa el-Fna in Marrakech at dinner time. The smells hit you first: argan oil, charcoal smoke, dried spices piled in bright cones, and the warm sweetness of pastilla drifting from somewhere nearby.

I spent two weeks eating my way through Morocco and came home with a completely different relationship to spice. Ras el hanout alone contains over twenty different spices. The preserved lemon in a slow-cooked tagine adds a brightness that no other ingredient replaces. The food is patient in a way that Western cooking rarely is.

posts.title: Five Dishes Every Home Cook Should Learn First
posts.body:
Most people want to cook better but do not know where to start. The mistake is reaching for complex recipes before understanding some fundamental techniques. Master five dishes properly and you will be able to cook well for the rest of your life.

The five I recommend: a properly seasoned pasta sauce from scratch, roast chicken (the technique transfers to almost everything), a simple vinaigrette you can make from memory, an omelette, and a one-pot braise. These cover the fundamental techniques of building flavour, understanding heat, emulsification, and patience.

posts.title: The Books That Permanently Changed How I Think
posts.body:
There are books you read and enjoy, and then there are books that restructure something fundamental about how you see the world. The second kind are rare, but when you encounter them they tend to leave a mark that does not fade.

The ones that did that for me include Thinking Fast and Slow, which made me aware of cognitive biases I had been operating under for years without knowing it, and The Remains of the Day, which taught me more about regret and self-deception through a fictional butler than any non-fiction book on the same subject ever could.

posts.title: Why Reading Fiction Makes You a Better Thinker
posts.body:
The case for fiction is often made on cultural grounds: it is enriching, it builds empathy, it preserves important stories. All true. But there is also a more practical argument that does not get made often enough: reading fiction is one of the best cognitive workouts available.

Following complex narratives with unreliable narrators, tracking multiple characters across long timelines, and inferring what characters mean rather than what they say all exercise mental muscles that transfer directly to real-world reasoning. Research consistently shows that regular fiction readers outperform non-readers on theory of mind tasks. It is not just entertainment.

posts.title: How I Built a Morning Routine That Actually Stuck
posts.body:
I have tried and abandoned dozens of morning routines. The problem was always designing them around what looked impressive rather than what I could realistically sustain. A 5am wake-up, meditation, journaling, a workout, and a cold shower before 7am looks great on paper and lasted me about four days.

What finally worked was starting with one small anchor habit, something so easy I could not say no. For me that was making coffee and sitting quietly for ten minutes without looking at my phone. From that anchor I gradually added other habits over several months until the routine felt natural rather than forced.

posts.title: Intermittent Fasting After One Year: Honest Results
posts.body:
I started intermittent fasting because I read too many enthusiastic testimonials online and wanted to see for myself. After a year of a 16:8 eating window, I have some honest observations that are more nuanced than most of what you will read.

The benefits for me were real: I think more clearly in the morning when I am not thinking about breakfast, my relationship with hunger changed from urgent to manageable, and I stopped snacking mindlessly in the evenings. The weight loss people talk about was modest for me. What changed more significantly was my overall relationship with food. I eat more intentionally now.

posts.title: Training for My First Half Marathon: What Surprised Me
posts.body:
I signed up for a half marathon knowing very little about distance running and immediately overcomplicated it. I bought a training plan, downloaded three different apps, obsessively tracked every run, and ended up injured five weeks in from overtraining.

The second attempt was simpler: three runs a week, one of them longer than the others, increasing total mileage by no more than 10 percent per week. That was essentially it. The mental challenge on race day turned out to be harder than the physical one. The last three kilometres were entirely a conversation between me and my own reluctance.

posts.title: Minimalism: What Happens After You Clear the Clutter
posts.body:
I spent a month getting rid of things I did not use or love. Books I was keeping out of obligation, clothes I had not worn in two years, kitchen gadgets that had lived in the back of a cupboard since I moved in. At the end of the month, I had donated four large bags and thrown away two more.

What surprised me was not how much lighter the apartment felt, though it did. It was how much mental energy I had been spending on objects I was not even consciously thinking about. Every possession is a small, unacknowledged decision you defer. Remove enough of them and the silence is genuinely noticeable.

posts.title: Why Sleep Is the Most Underrated Performance Tool
posts.body:
Every productivity conversation eventually touches on sleep but rarely stays there long. We talk about it briefly, acknowledge it is important, and then move on to discussing tools, systems, and habits. This is backwards. Sleep is not one factor among many. It is the foundation everything else runs on.

Seven to nine hours is not a guideline, it is a biological requirement. During sleep your brain processes the day's information, consolidates memories, and clears metabolic waste products. The research on sleep deprivation is alarming: two weeks of sleeping six hours a night produces cognitive impairment equivalent to two full nights of no sleep. Most people who are chronically under-slept have no accurate sense of how impaired they actually are.

posts.title: I Meditated Every Day for Thirty Days: Here Is What I Found
posts.body:
I went into the thirty-day meditation challenge as a sceptic with a reasonable prior: the science looks promising but the wellness culture around it is exhausting. I committed to ten minutes a day with a simple breath-focus technique and kept notes throughout.

The most significant change was not the calm that meditation advocates describe, though that came eventually. It was noticing my own thinking more clearly. I became more aware of when I was anxious before the anxiety became overwhelming. I caught myself catastrophising in real time and could sometimes interrupt it. That gap between stimulus and response became slightly wider. Whether that is mindfulness or just paying more attention, I am not sure it matters.

posts.title: The Three Camera Settings That Actually Matter
posts.body:
Photography tutorials love to overwhelm beginners with technical information. In reality, understanding three settings and how they interact gives you control over 90 percent of what makes a photograph work or fail: aperture, shutter speed, and ISO.

Aperture controls how much light enters the lens and how much of the scene is in focus. Shutter speed controls how long the sensor is exposed and whether motion is frozen or blurred. ISO controls the sensitivity to light and how much grain appears in the image. The exposure triangle is just the relationship between these three. Change one and you need to compensate with another.

posts.title: Composition Rules That Transform Ordinary Photos
posts.body:
Technical settings matter, but composition is what separates a photograph from a snapshot. The good news is that most strong compositions follow a small number of principles that can be learned quickly.

The rule of thirds is the starting point: divide your frame into a 3x3 grid and place your subject near the intersections rather than dead centre. Leading lines pull the eye through the image. Negative space gives your subject room to breathe. Framing within the frame uses elements in the scene to draw attention to your subject. None of these are rules in a strict sense. They are just patterns that the eye tends to find satisfying.

posts.title: What Camera Gear Do You Actually Need?
posts.body:
The camera gear question is one of the most reliably misleading conversations in photography. Forum threads run to hundreds of replies debating the difference between cameras that, in real-world shooting conditions, produce images most people cannot distinguish in a blind test.

Here is a more useful framing: the best camera is the one you have with you. A phone camera used well will produce better images than a professional camera used badly. The one piece of gear that makes a genuine difference for most photographers is not the camera body but a good prime lens, preferably a 50mm or 35mm equivalent. Fixed focal length forces you to think about composition instead of zooming your way to a shot.

posts.title: Street Photography: How to Stop Being Afraid of Your Subject
posts.body:
The hardest part of street photography is not the camera settings. It is the moment before you press the shutter when you are standing in front of a stranger and your entire nervous system is telling you to lower the camera and walk away.

Most street photographers report that the fear never fully goes away; it just becomes manageable with experience. The practical advice is to start in busy public spaces where no one is paying attention to you, shoot from the hip until you build confidence, and understand the legal framework in your country. In most public spaces you have the legal right to photograph people. Knowing that helps.

posts.title: Photo Editing: How to Develop a Consistent Style
posts.body:
Raw files from any modern camera look flat and unimpressive straight out of the camera. This is intentional. The raw format captures as much information as possible and hands the interpretation to you. Editing is not cheating; it is part of the photographic process, and always has been.

The most efficient way to develop a consistent style is to start with a preset you like as a baseline, then adjust from there. Pay most attention to white balance, contrast, and how you handle shadows and highlights. The specific numbers matter less than applying the same approach consistently across your work. Consistency is what makes a portfolio feel coherent.

posts.title: Night Photography: Making Darkness Work for You
posts.body:
Most people put the camera away when the sun goes down. This is a mistake. The hour after sunset and the hour before sunrise produce some of the most interesting light available, and the city at night offers textures and moods that are impossible to capture in daylight.

For night photography you need a tripod, or at minimum a stable surface. Long exposures blur moving cars into light trails and turn choppy water glassy smooth. Use your lowest native ISO to minimise noise and expose to the right of the histogram without clipping highlights. The technical side becomes second nature quickly. The harder part is learning to see compositions in the dark.

posts.title: Portrait Photography: Light Is Everything
posts.body:
I have seen portraits taken with expensive studio equipment that looked worse than portraits taken with a single window and a reflective surface. Equipment matters less than understanding how light wraps around a face.

Natural light from a large north-facing window is some of the best portrait light available for free. Keep your subject close to the window for short, dramatic light or move them back for something softer. A reflector, even a white piece of card, fills in shadows on the opposite side of the face. The eyes are what the viewer goes to first in any portrait. If the eyes are sharp and the light is in them, the portrait will work.

posts.title: How I Got Serious About Photography (And What I Wish I Had Known)
posts.body:
I bought my first serious camera eight years ago and spent the first two years taking technically competent photographs of nothing interesting. Sharp images of empty benches, well-exposed skies, correctly exposed sunsets. The technical side improved quickly. The eye for a subject took much longer.

The shift happened when I stopped asking myself what would make a technically good photograph and started asking what I actually found interesting, strange, or beautiful about a particular scene. The camera then becomes a way of answering that question rather than an end in itself. If you are starting out, my strongest advice is to shoot subjects you genuinely care about, even if the technical execution is rough.

comments.body: The hardest part is exactly what you say: learning to see compositions in the dark. My eyes adjusted to finding shapes and light differently after a few months of regular night shooting.

comments.name: Yara Mansour
comments.body: The window light point cannot be overstated. I have seen professional portrait photographers choose a simple window over expensive studio equipment because the quality of light is genuinely better.

comments.name: Jake Svensson
comments.body: The eyes being the first thing the viewer goes to is why sharp focus on the eyes is non-negotiable even when other parts of the image are soft.

comments.name: Nia Addo
comments.body: The card reflector is one of the highest value-per-cost tools in photography. I used a white foam board for two years before buying anything more sophisticated.

comments.name: Pavel Horak
comments.body: A large north-facing window is the ultimate portrait light. Soft, diffused, and consistent throughout the day. If I could only choose one light source it would be that.

comments.name: Serena Volta
comments.body: The shift from asking what makes a technically good photograph to asking what you find interesting is the exact transition I went through. The camera becomes a different tool after that.

comments.name: Kwame Asante
comments.body: Shooting subjects you genuinely care about is the advice that resonates most. Technical competence in the service of something you actually want to say produces much better work.

comments.name: Irene Bouchard
comments.body: Two years of technically competent photographs of nothing interesting is such an honest description of the early phase. Almost every photographer goes through it.

comments.name: Dani Reiter
comments.body: The question about what you find strange or beautiful is a genuinely useful frame. I have started asking it before raising the camera and it changes what I actually photograph.
